title: Loops in C# and When to Use Each
interviewQuestion: Explain the different loop types in C# and when you'd use each one.

story.setup: A factory floor has four different workers, each suited to a specific repetitive task.
scenes: One worker counts down a numbered rack of parts from the last slot to the first — she needs the index at every step, so she uses a for loop, the only loop built for that kind of counted, indexable control.

Another worker keeps dividing a stack of coins by 10 until nothing's left, with no idea in advance how many rounds it'll take — that's a while loop: stop when a condition says stop, and it might run zero times if the stack starts empty.

A third worker at the door keeps asking visitors for ID until one is finally valid — but he has to ask at least ONCE no matter what, so it's a do-while: the body runs first, THEN the condition is checked.

The fourth worker is handed a box of mixed parts with no numbers on them at all — a Dictionary, a HashSet — so counting by index is impossible; he just picks up each part in turn with foreach, which works on anything enumerable.
story.moral: for is for counted/indexed work, while is for unknown-length work gated by a condition, do-while guarantees at least one run, and foreach is for visiting every item of any enumerable collection safely.

analogy: for is counting down a numbered rack by index; while is dividing coins until none are left; do-while is asking for ID at least once before checking it; foreach is picking items from an unlabeled box one by one.
explanation: for is the right choice when the count is known in advance or you need the index during iteration, and it can run zero times. while is the right choice when the number of repetitions is unknown ahead of time and depends on a condition evaluated each time, and it too can run zero times if the condition starts false. do-while behaves like while, except the body always executes at least once because the condition is checked after the body runs, which fits scenarios like prompting for input where you must ask before you can validate. foreach visits every item of a collection without needing an index at all, which makes it the only option for index-less collections like Dictionary and HashSet, and it protects against off-by-one bugs — but it cannot modify the collection while iterating (an InvalidOperationException is thrown if you try), its loop variable is read-only, and it only moves forward.
interviewAnswerShort: Use for when you know the count or need an index, while when the number of iterations is unknown and gated by a condition, do-while when the body must run at least once, and foreach to visit every item of any collection — especially index-less ones like Dictionary and HashSet.
interviewAnswerDetailed: C# provides four loop constructs, each suited to a different shape of problem. for is used when the number of iterations is known upfront or when you need explicit control over the index — for example, iterating an array backwards with `for (int i = arr.Length - 1; i >= 0; i--)`, which only for can express cleanly; its minimum run count is zero, since the initial condition check can immediately fail. while is used when the stopping condition depends on something evaluated during the loop rather than a fixed count, such as `while (n > 0) { n /= 10; digits++; }` to count digits — the stop signal is effectively an event that happens mid-computation, and like for it can run zero times if the condition starts false. do-while is identical to while except the condition is checked after the body executes, guaranteeing at least one run — the natural fit for 'ask, then judge' patterns like `do { input = Console.ReadLine(); } while (!IsValid(input));`, where you must obtain input before you can validate it. foreach visits every element of anything implementing IEnumerable<T> without any index at all, which is the only loop that can walk collections with no inherent index, like Dictionary<K,V> or HashSet<T> — a for loop physically cannot iterate those without first converting them to something indexable. Loops exist fundamentally so you can write logic once and run it N times: processing collections of unknown size, searching, accumulating (sum/count/max), retrying until success, or reading input whose length isn't known at compile time — LINQ, foreach, and SQL row-by-row processing are all loops underneath their higher-level syntax. foreach is generally preferred over for when working with collections because it eliminates off-by-one bugs and works uniformly across indexed and non-indexed collections, but it comes with real constraints: you cannot add or remove items from the collection while iterating it (doing so throws InvalidOperationException because the underlying enumerator detects the collection was modified), the iteration variable itself is read-only within the loop body, and it can only move forward — you cannot skip backward or jump around as you can with a for loop's index.

codeExample.explanation: Each loop fits a different shape of problem: indexed traversal, unknown-length condition-gated work, must-run-once input prompting, and index-less collection iteration.

mistakes: Trying to use a plain for loop to iterate a Dictionary or HashSet -- they have no index; foreach is required.
Adding or removing items from a collection while inside a foreach over it, causing InvalidOperationException.
Reaching for do-while when a normal while would do -- do-while's 'runs at least once' guarantee is easy to misuse where zero runs was actually intended.
Assigning to the foreach loop variable, which the compiler disallows since it's read-only.
Using while(true) with a manual break instead of expressing the actual stopping condition directly, hurting readability.

followUps.question: Why do we use loops at all?
followUps.answer: To write logic once and run it N times. Real uses: processing collections of unknown size, searching, accumulating (sum/count/max), retrying until success, reading input whose length isn't known at compile time. LINQ, foreach, and SQL row processing are all loops underneath.

followUps.question: Why choose foreach over for?
followUps.answer: No off-by-one bugs, and it works on collections with no index at all (Dictionary, HashSet, LINQ results) -- a for loop physically cannot walk those. Limits: you can't modify the collection while iterating (InvalidOperationException), the loop variable is read-only, and it's forward-only.

followUps.question: What's the minimum number of times each loop can run?
followUps.answer: for: 0. while: 0. do-while: 1 (body always runs before the condition is first checked). foreach: 0, if the collection is empty.

memoryHack.oneLiner: for = count the rack by index; while = divide until empty; do-while = ask then judge; foreach = pick from an unlabeled box.
memoryHack.mnemonic: FWDF: For-index, While-condition, Do-once-guaranteed, Foreach-any-collection.
memoryHack.memoryPalace: Picture a factory floor: a worker counting a numbered rack backward (for), one dividing coins until the pile's gone (while), a bouncer who must check ID at least once before judging (do-while), and someone reaching into an unlabeled box item by item (foreach).

bestPractices: Default to foreach for collection iteration unless you specifically need the index or reverse traversal.
Use for when the index itself is part of the logic (backwards iteration, skipping by steps, array manipulation).
Use do-while only when the body genuinely must execute at least once before the condition can be evaluated.
Never mutate a collection you're foreach-ing over; collect changes in a separate list and apply them after the loop.
Prefer LINQ methods over manual loops when the intent is a transformation/filter/aggregate and readability improves.
performanceTips: foreach over an array or List<T> is JIT-optimized nearly identically to an equivalent for loop -- don't over-optimize by hand for common collections.
foreach over an IEnumerable<T> that isn't a List/array (like a LINQ query) re-evaluates lazily each iteration -- materialize with .ToList() first if you'll iterate multiple times.
for loops avoid the enumerator allocation that foreach on certain custom IEnumerable implementations may incur, relevant in very hot paths.

quiz.explanation: do-while checks its condition after executing the body, so the body always runs at least once regardless of the condition.

options: Dictionary has no inherent index to loop over
It's technically possible and common practice
quiz.explanation: Dictionary entries live in hash buckets, not a sequential index, so there's no numeric index for a for loop to use -- foreach is required.

quiz.question: What happens if you add an item to a List<T> while foreach-ing over it?
options: It silently skips the new item
quiz.explanation: Modifying a collection during foreach iteration invalidates the enumerator's version check, throwing InvalidOperationException.

flashcards.back: Known count or when you need the index during iteration.
Unknown number of iterations, gated by a condition; can run zero times.
Same as while, but the body must run at least once (checked after).
Visiting every item of any collection, especially index-less ones like Dictionary/HashSet.

flashcards.back: InvalidOperationException is thrown.

Loops exist so logic can be written once and executed N times -- processing collections, searching, accumulating totals, retrying until success, or reading input of unknown length; LINQ, foreach, and row-by-row SQL processing are all loops under the hood. foreach's real constraints are worth remembering: you cannot add or remove items from the collection while iterating it, which throws InvalidOperationException; the loop variable is read-only; and iteration only moves forward, unlike a for loop's freely controllable index.

title: The using Keyword
interviewQuestion: What does the using keyword do in C#, and why does it matter for resource management?

story.setup: A hotel has a strict rule: every guest who checks out a room key MUST return it, no matter how their stay ends.
scenes: The front desk clerk keeps a master directory of services (using System.Linq;) — that's the import meaning, just naming which departments exist.

A guest checks in with a using block: using (var conn = new SqlConnection(cs)) { ... } — no matter what happens during the stay, even if the guest causes a fire alarm (an exception), the room key is guaranteed to be returned the moment they leave the block. Compiles to try { } finally { conn?.Dispose(); }.

A frequent guest prefers the shorter check-in form — using var conn = new SqlConnection(cs); — same guarantee, but the key auto-returns at the end of the whole visit (scope) instead of a nested block.

If a guest just walks off with the key and never returns it — skipping using entirely — the hotel eventually runs out of spare keys for new guests. That's connection pool exhaustion: the classic 'the API suddenly got slow' bug caused by unreturned DB connections.
story.moral: using guarantees Dispose() runs even when an exception is thrown, which is essential for unmanaged resources like DB connections, file handles, and sockets that the GC does not clean up on your schedule.

analogy: using is a hotel's mandatory key-return policy — no matter how the stay ends, the key (unmanaged resource) is guaranteed to be handed back the moment the guest's block or scope ends.
explanation: using has three related meanings in C#. As a namespace import, `using System.Linq;`, global using, and using aliases bring types into scope. As a using statement, `using (var conn = new SqlConnection(cs)) { ... }` guarantees Dispose() is called on conn the moment the block ends, even if an exception is thrown inside it — it compiles to `try { } finally { conn?.Dispose(); }`. As a using declaration (C# 8+), `using var conn = new SqlConnection(cs);` disposes the object at the end of the enclosing scope without requiring a nested block, reducing indentation. This matters because the garbage collector manages memory but not unmanaged resources — file handles, database connections, sockets — and a missing using on something like a database connection causes connection pool exhaustion, a classic root cause of an API that mysteriously becomes slow or unresponsive under load. The async version, await using, disposes objects implementing IAsyncDisposable asynchronously.
interviewAnswerShort: using guarantees Dispose() is called deterministically — even if an exception occurs — which is essential for unmanaged resources like DB connections and file handles that the garbage collector does not reliably clean up on a predictable schedule.
interviewAnswerDetailed: The using keyword serves three distinct purposes in C#. First, as a namespace import — `using System.Linq;`, `global using` for solution-wide imports, or `using Alias = Some.Long.Namespace;` for aliasing — it simply brings types into scope and has nothing to do with resource cleanup. Second, as a using statement, `using (var conn = new SqlConnection(cs)) { ... }` wraps the enclosed block so that conn.Dispose() is guaranteed to run when the block exits, whether normally or via an exception — the compiler literally lowers this to `try { ... } finally { conn?.Dispose(); }`, giving deterministic, guaranteed cleanup regardless of control flow. Third, the using declaration introduced in C# 8 — `using var conn = new SqlConnection(cs);` — achieves the same guaranteed disposal but ties it to the end of the enclosing scope (typically the method) rather than requiring an explicit nested block, which reduces indentation for the common case of 'use this resource for the rest of the method.' The reason this matters deeply is that .NET's garbage collector only manages managed memory — it has no knowledge of unmanaged resources like open file handles, database connections, network sockets, or GDI handles, and finalizers that could eventually clean these up run on the GC's schedule, not yours, which can be arbitrarily delayed. Forgetting to dispose a database connection, for example, doesn't necessarily crash immediately — instead, the connection pool for that database gradually exhausts its available connections as old ones are never returned, and new requests start blocking or timing out waiting for a free connection, which is one of the most classic 'the API suddenly got slow (or hangs) under load' production bugs, often invisible in development where load is low. Any type implementing IDisposable should be wrapped in using (or a using declaration) at its point of use. For asynchronous disposal — types implementing IAsyncDisposable, such as some database or stream types with async cleanup logic — the async counterpart await using ensures the asynchronous DisposeAsync() is awaited properly rather than blocking a thread.

codeExample.explanation: Both the using statement and using declaration guarantee Dispose() runs even on exceptions; await using does the same for IAsyncDisposable types.

mistakes: Forgetting to wrap an IDisposable resource (SqlConnection, FileStream, HttpClient instances misused per-request) in using, risking leaked handles or pool exhaustion.

Using HttpClient with a using block per request -- HttpClient itself should typically be long-lived/shared (e.g., via IHttpClientFactory), not disposed per call, to avoid socket exhaustion, a different but related resource problem.
Assuming the garbage collector will promptly clean up unmanaged resources -- it doesn't, and finalizer-based cleanup is delayed and non-deterministic.
Nesting many using statements instead of using the more readable using declaration (C# 8+) where a single flat scope suffices.
Forgetting await using for IAsyncDisposable types, causing improper or blocking disposal of async resources.

followUps.answer: A using statement (using (...) { ... }) disposes at the end of its explicit block. A using declaration (C# 8+, using var conn = ...;) disposes at the end of the enclosing scope instead, avoiding a nested block and reducing indentation.

title: Constructor and Destructor
interviewQuestion: What is a constructor and a destructor in C#, and should you use destructors in modern code?

story.setup: A hotel room has a check-in ritual and, separately, a room that eventually gets torn down when the whole building is demolished.
scenes: The moment a guest checks in, the front desk runs a fixed ritual — same name as the room type, executed automatically — making the bed, setting the thermostat, stocking the minibar. That's the constructor: same name as the class, runs on creation, initializes state.

Nobody schedules exactly when the wrecking crew tears down an abandoned wing of the hotel — it happens whenever the demolition company (the GC) eventually gets around to it, on no fixed timetable. That's the destructor/finalizer (~ClassName()): you can't call it or predict when it runs.

A wing scheduled for demolition doesn't come down immediately — it first sits on a 'condemned buildings' list for an extra inspection cycle before the wrecking ball ever swings. That's the finalization queue: having a finalizer delays collection by a full GC cycle.

The smart approach is a scheduled housekeeping checkout instead — using + IDisposable — where the guest's stuff (unmanaged handles) is definitely cleaned up the moment they leave, on a predictable schedule, not whenever demolition eventually happens.
story.moral: Constructors run deterministically on creation; destructors/finalizers run unpredictably on GC collection and should almost never be used in modern C# — IDisposable + using gives deterministic cleanup instead.

analogy: A constructor is a hotel's automatic check-in ritual, run the instant a guest arrives; a destructor is an abandoned wing torn down whenever the demolition crew (the GC) eventually gets to it — with no fixed schedule.
explanation: A constructor shares the same name as its class, runs automatically when an instance is created, and is responsible for initializing the object's state — it can be parameterless or parameterized, and a class can have multiple overloaded constructors. A destructor, written as ~ClassName() and formally called a finalizer, runs when the garbage collector decides to collect the object; you cannot call it directly and cannot predict when it will run, since GC timing is non-deterministic. In modern C# you should almost never write a finalizer: having one delays an object's actual collection by a full extra GC cycle, because finalizable objects are placed on a separate finalization queue and processed before their memory can truly be reclaimed. The correct pattern for deterministic cleanup is implementing IDisposable and using it with the using keyword; if you genuinely must have a finalizer (typically only for wrapping raw unmanaged handles directly), you should implement the full Dispose pattern and call GC.SuppressFinalize(this) inside Dispose() to tell the GC the finalizer is no longer needed once cleanup has already happened deterministically.
interviewAnswerShort: A constructor initializes an object's state deterministically at creation time and shares the class's name; a destructor (finalizer, ~ClassName()) runs unpredictably whenever the GC eventually collects the object, and modern C# almost never uses them directly, preferring IDisposable and using for deterministic cleanup.
interviewAnswerDetailed: A constructor is a special method with the same name as its containing class, invoked automatically the moment an object is instantiated with new, and its job is to put the object into a valid initial state — setting default field values, validating arguments, or wiring up dependencies; a class can define multiple constructors with different parameter lists (constructor overloading), and one constructor can call another via `: this(...)`. A destructor, syntactically `~ClassName()` and technically called a finalizer, is the counterpart the CLR invokes when it decides to garbage-collect the object — critically, you have no way to call it directly and no way to predict or control when the garbage collector will actually run it, since GC timing depends on memory pressure and generation promotion, not your code's logic. Modern C# guidance is to almost never write a finalizer: any object with a finalizer is placed on a special finalization queue when the GC would otherwise reclaim it, and it survives an additional full garbage collection cycle before its memory is actually freed, since the finalizer thread must run first — this measurably delays memory reclamation across every object with a finalizer, not just the ones actually holding scarce unmanaged resources. Because of this, the standard, correct way to release resources deterministically — as soon as you're done with them, on your own schedule rather than the GC's — is to implement IDisposable and consume the type through using or a using declaration, which guarantees Dispose() runs even if an exception occurs. If you genuinely do need a finalizer, which is rare and typically limited to types wrapping raw unmanaged handles directly (rather than through a SafeHandle, which is usually the better approach), you should implement the full Dispose pattern: a public Dispose() method, a protected virtual Dispose(bool disposing) that both the public Dispose() and the finalizer call, and critically, GC.SuppressFinalize(this) called inside the public Dispose() method — this tells the runtime that cleanup has already happened deterministically, so the finalizer doesn't need to run and the object can skip the finalization queue entirely, avoiding that extra GC cycle penalty.

codeExample.explanation: Report's finalizer runs at an unpredictable GC-driven time; SafeResource shows the preferred pattern -- deterministic Dispose() plus GC.SuppressFinalize to avoid the extra finalization cycle entirely.

mistakes: Writing a finalizer for a type that doesn't hold raw unmanaged resources -- it just adds GC overhead with no benefit.
Assuming a destructor/finalizer runs promptly (like at the end of scope) -- it runs whenever the GC decides to, which could be much later or, at process exit, not at all in a predictable order.

Forgetting GC.SuppressFinalize(this) in the Dispose pattern when a finalizer is present, causing the object to still go through the finalization queue unnecessarily even after Dispose() already cleaned up.
Relying on a finalizer instead of IDisposable + using for resources that need timely release (like file handles or connections).
Calling a destructor directly (e.g., obj.~ClassName()) -- this is not valid C# syntax; finalizers can never be called explicitly.

followUps.question: Should you use destructors in modern C#?
followUps.answer: Almost never. A finalizer delays collection by a full GC cycle (the object goes on the finalization queue). Use IDisposable + using for deterministic cleanup. If you must have one (raw unmanaged handles), implement the full Dispose pattern and call GC.SuppressFinalize(this).

followUps.question: What's the full Dispose pattern?
followUps.answer: A public parameterless Dispose() that calls a protected virtual Dispose(bool disposing), which both the public Dispose() and (optionally) the finalizer call -- the bool distinguishes deterministic disposal from finalizer-driven cleanup so managed resources are only touched during deterministic disposal. The public Dispose() also calls GC.SuppressFinalize(this) so the finalizer doesn't need to run.

followUps.question: Can a struct have a destructor?
followUps.answer: No -- finalizers are only valid on classes (reference types); structs are value types and don't participate in GC-driven finalization since they don't live independently on the heap in the way classes do.

memoryHack.oneLiner: Constructor = automatic check-in ritual; destructor = a demolition crew's own unpredictable schedule.
memoryHack.mnemonic: CD: Constructor = Certain timing; Destructor = Delayed/uncertain timing.
memoryHack.memoryPalace: Picture a hotel: check-in happens instantly and predictably every time (constructor), while an abandoned wing sits on a condemned list waiting for the demolition crew to eventually show up on their own schedule (finalizer) -- versus a guest who checks out properly and the room is cleaned immediately (IDisposable + using).

bestPractices: Prefer IDisposable + using for any resource that needs timely, deterministic release.
Avoid writing finalizers unless you're directly wrapping a raw unmanaged handle (prefer SafeHandle where possible, which already implements this correctly).
If you do implement a finalizer, always call GC.SuppressFinalize(this) in your public Dispose() to skip the extra finalization cycle once cleanup is done.
Use constructor overloading and : this(...) chaining to avoid duplicating initialization logic across constructors.
Validate constructor arguments early (guard clauses) so objects can never exist in an invalid state.
performanceTips: Every object with a finalizer survives an extra GC generation/cycle before its memory is actually reclaimed -- avoid finalizers unless truly necessary.
GC.SuppressFinalize(this) inside Dispose() avoids that extra finalization overhead once you've already cleaned up deterministically.
Constructors that do expensive work (I/O, heavy computation) can make object creation surprisingly costly -- keep constructors lightweight and defer expensive work to explicit methods where possible.

quiz.explanation: Objects with finalizers are queued for finalization and require an additional GC pass, delaying actual memory reclamation.

quiz.question: What is the modern recommended way to handle deterministic resource cleanup?
options: Implement IDisposable and use the using keyword
Rely on the constructor to also clean up
quiz.explanation: IDisposable combined with using (or a using declaration) guarantees deterministic cleanup, avoiding the unpredictability and overhead of finalizers.

Runs when the GC eventually collects the object; timing is unpredictable, can't be called directly.

title: Access Modifiers
interviewQuestion: What are the access modifiers in C#, and what does each one control?

story.setup: A corporate office building has clearance levels controlling exactly who can enter each room.
scenes: The public lobby (public) is open to anyone from any company visiting the building.
A private office (private) only its own occupant can enter — the default clearance for any room unless marked otherwise.

A protected family vault (protected) opens for the owner AND their direct descendants — same class plus derived classes — while an internal department floor (internal) opens to anyone badge-registered with THIS company but locked to outside visitors, the default for whole classes.

A protected internal conference room opens wider still — ANYONE in the building (same assembly) OR any descendant company anywhere (derived classes, even other assemblies), an OR condition — while a private protected archive is stricter, open only to descendant departments ALSO badge-registered with this exact company, an AND condition.
And a file-only whisper room (file, C# 11+) is so private its walls don't even exist outside the one blueprint page (source file) it was drawn on.
story.moral: Each access modifier is a clearance level controlling exactly which code can see a member — start with the narrowest clearance (private) and widen only when a real need forces it.

analogy: Access modifiers are building clearance levels — public is the open lobby, private is your own locked office, protected is a family vault open to descendants, internal is a department floor open only within the company.
explanation: public is accessible from anywhere. private is accessible only inside the same class, and is the default access level for class members if none is specified. protected is accessible from the same class plus any derived classes. internal is accessible from anywhere within the same assembly, and is the default access level for top-level classes. protected internal is accessible from the same assembly OR from derived classes anywhere, even in other assemblies — an OR condition, making it wider than either protected or internal alone. private protected (C# 7.2+) is accessible only from derived classes within the same assembly — an AND condition, making it narrower than protected internal. file (C# 11+) restricts a type's visibility to the same source file only. The rule of thumb: start with private and widen access only when a real need requires it — this discipline is the core mechanism behind encapsulation.
interviewAnswerShort: public is open to everyone, private is the same class only, protected adds derived classes, internal adds the same assembly, protected internal is same-assembly OR derived-anywhere, and private protected is derived-classes-within-the-same-assembly-only — start private and widen only as needed.
interviewAnswerDetailed: C# provides seven access levels controlling visibility. public members are accessible from any code that can see the type at all. private members — the default for class members when no modifier is specified — are accessible only within the declaring class itself, not even from derived classes. protected members extend that to the declaring class plus any classes that derive from it, anywhere. internal members — the default for top-level class declarations — are accessible anywhere within the same compiled assembly, but not from other assemblies referencing it. protected internal combines protected and internal with OR semantics: a member is accessible either from anywhere in the same assembly, or from any derived class regardless of which assembly it's in — this makes it the widest of the compound modifiers. private protected (introduced in C# 7.2) combines them with AND semantics instead: a member is accessible only from derived classes that are ALSO within the same assembly — narrower than either protected or internal alone, and useful when you want to expose something to your own library's subclasses without letting external assemblies' derived classes see it too. file (introduced in C# 11) is the newest and narrowest, restricting a type's visibility to the exact source file it's declared in — useful for source-generator-emitted helper types that shouldn't leak into the rest of the assembly. The consistent rule of thumb across all of these is to start every member as private and only widen its accessibility when a concrete need forces you to — this discipline of minimal necessary exposure is the actual mechanism that implements encapsulation, one of the core OOP pillars, since it prevents external code from depending on or corrupting internal implementation details.

codeExample.code:
public class Account
{
    private decimal _balance;                 // same class only
    protected void Audit() { }                 // same class + derived classes
    internal void ResetForTests() { }           // same assembly
    protected internal void Notify() { }        // same assembly OR derived anywhere
    private protected void InternalAudit() { }  // derived classes, same assembly only
}

file class HelperOnlyInThisFile { }              // C# 11+, this source file only
codeExample.explanation: Each modifier narrows or widens visibility along the class/assembly/inheritance axes -- private is narrowest, public is widest, and the compound modifiers combine assembly and inheritance scope differently.

mistakes: Confusing protected internal (OR -- wider) with private protected (AND -- narrower) -- these are commonly swapped in interviews.
Making members public by default instead of starting private and widening deliberately, which breaks encapsulation.
Forgetting that private is the default for class members but internal is the default for top-level classes.

Assuming protected members are accessible from any code that has an instance of the class -- they're only accessible from within the class or its derived classes' own code, not via an arbitrary external reference.
Not realizing file-scoped types (file, C# 11+) can't be referenced at all outside their declaring source file, even within the same assembly.

followUps.question: What's the difference between protected internal and private protected?
followUps.answer: protected internal accessible from Same assembly OR derived classes anywhere -- wider (OR). private protected accessible from derived classes within the same assembly only -- narrower (AND).

followUps.question: What are the default access levels if you omit a modifier?
followUps.answer: private for class members, internal for top-level class/type declarations.

followUps.question: Why would you use private protected over just protected?
followUps.answer: To expose a member to your own library's derived classes while explicitly preventing derived classes defined in OTHER assemblies (e.g., by third-party consumers of a NuGet package) from accessing it -- protected alone would allow any external derived class to see it, while private protected keeps it strictly in-house.

memoryHack.oneLiner: Access modifiers are office building clearance levels -- start locked (private), widen only as needed.
memoryHack.mnemonic: PPPIPP-F: Public, Private, Protected, Internal, Protected-internal(OR), Private-protected(AND), File.
memoryHack.memoryPalace: Picture an office tower: an open lobby (public), your own locked office (private), a family vault open to descendants (protected), a company-only floor (internal), a wide-open OR-conference-room (protected internal), a strict AND-archive (private protected), and a whisper room that doesn't exist outside one blueprint page (file).

bestPractices: Default every new member to private, and widen only when a concrete consumer genuinely needs broader access.
Use internal for implementation details that should be shared across your assembly but hidden from consumers of your public API.
Use protected internal sparingly and deliberately -- it's the widest compound modifier and can leak implementation details to external derived classes.
Prefer private protected over protected when you want to expose something only to your own library's derived classes, not third-party ones.
Use file-scoped types for source-generator output or truly file-local helper types that shouldn't be referenceable elsewhere.
performanceTips: Access modifiers are a compile-time/JIT concept with no runtime performance cost -- choose based on encapsulation needs, not performance.
Tighter access (private/internal) can enable more aggressive JIT inlining and devirtualization in some cases since the compiler can reason about all possible callers.
Minimizing public surface area reduces the API contract you must maintain backward compatibility for across versions.

quiz.question: Which access modifier is the default for class members if none is specified?
quiz.explanation: private is the default access level for class members when no modifier is explicitly written.

quiz.question: How does protected internal differ from private protected?
options: protected internal is same-assembly OR derived-anywhere (wider); private protected is derived-classes-within-same-assembly (narrower)
protected internal is narrower than private protected
quiz.explanation: protected internal combines the two conditions with OR (wider access); private protected combines them with AND (narrower access).

quiz.question: What does the file access modifier (C# 11+) restrict a type to?
options: The exact source file it's declared in
quiz.explanation: file restricts a type's visibility to only the source file where it's declared, even within the same assembly.

flashcards.front: What does internal restrict access to?
flashcards.back: The same assembly only -- default for top-level classes.
Same assembly OR derived anywhere -- OR, wider.
Derived classes within the same assembly -- AND, narrower.

flashcards.front: What's the rule of thumb for choosing access modifiers?
flashcards.back: Start private, widen only when required -- the mechanism behind encapsulation.

Rule: start private, widen only as needed.
revision2min: C# has seven access levels. public is open to any code that can see the type. private -- the default for class members -- restricts access to the declaring class only, not even derived classes. protected extends that to the declaring class plus any derived classes anywhere. internal -- the default for top-level classes -- opens access to the entire containing assembly but nothing outside it. protected internal combines the two with OR semantics: accessible from the same assembly, or from any derived class regardless of assembly -- the widest compound modifier. private protected (C# 7.2+) combines them with AND semantics instead: accessible only from derived classes that are also within the same assembly, useful for exposing something to your own library's subclasses while excluding derived classes defined by external consumers. file (C# 11+) is the narrowest, restricting a type to the exact source file it's declared in, useful for source-generator helper types. The consistent guiding principle across all of these is to start every member as private and widen deliberately only when a genuine need arises -- this discipline of minimal necessary exposure is precisely the mechanism that implements encapsulation, preventing external code from depending on or corrupting a type's internal state.

summary: C#'s access modifiers form a spectrum of encapsulation from private (same class) to public (everywhere), with protected internal (OR) and private protected (AND) giving fine-grained control across the assembly and inheritance axes.

title: Serialization and Deserialization
interviewQuestion: What is serialization and deserialization in C#, and where is it used in real applications?

story.setup: A live object in memory is like a fully assembled piece of furniture — great in the room, useless for shipping.
scenes: To ship it across the country (over the network), the furniture must be disassembled into flat-packed parts with an instruction sheet — that's serialization: converting an object into a transferable format like JSON, XML, or binary.
string json = JsonSerializer.Serialize(student); flattens the live Student object into readable text: {"Id":1,"Name":"Raj"}.

At the destination, someone follows the instruction sheet to reassemble the exact same piece of furniture — that's deserialization: Student s = JsonSerializer.Deserialize<Student>(json); turns the flat-packed data back into a live object.

Every Web API does this constantly and invisibly — every response you send gets flat-packed to JSON before it leaves the server, and every request body arriving gets reassembled into a live C# object before your controller ever touches it.
story.moral: Serialization flattens a live object into a transferable, storable format; deserialization reconstructs it — this round trip is the invisible backbone of every Web API request and response.

analogy: Serialization is flat-packing furniture for shipping; deserialization is assembling it back into a usable piece at the destination.
explanation: Serialization converts an in-memory object into a transferable or storable format such as JSON, XML, or binary; deserialization reverses the process, reconstructing an equivalent object from that format. In modern .NET, System.Text.Json's JsonSerializer.Serialize(obj) converts an object graph to a JSON string, and JsonSerializer.Deserialize<T>(json) parses that JSON back into an instance of type T. This round trip underlies virtually every Web API: incoming HTTP request bodies are deserialized into C# model/DTO objects before a controller action runs, and objects returned from an action are serialized into the HTTP response body that the client receives, typically as JSON for REST APIs.
interviewAnswerShort: Serialization converts an in-memory object into a transferable format like JSON, XML, or binary; deserialization converts it back — every Web API request body is deserialized into a C# object and every response object is serialized before it's sent.
interviewAnswerDetailed: Serialization is the process of converting a live, in-memory object graph into a format that can be transmitted over a network, written to disk, or stored in a database — common formats include JSON (the dominant choice for modern web APIs), XML (still common in enterprise/legacy interop and SOAP-based systems), and binary formats (compact but less portable and now largely discouraged for cross-platform or cross-version scenarios due to security and versioning concerns). Deserialization is the reverse operation: taking that transferable representation and reconstructing an equivalent object in memory. In modern .NET, the built-in System.Text.Json namespace provides JsonSerializer.Serialize(myObject), which walks the object's public properties and produces a JSON string like `{"Id":1,"Name":"Raj"}`, and JsonSerializer.Deserialize<Student>(json), which parses that JSON text and constructs a new Student instance with matching property values. This pattern is the invisible backbone of essentially every Web API built on ASP.NET Core: when a client sends a POST request with a JSON body, ASP.NET Core's model binding deserializes that JSON into the strongly-typed parameter of your controller action before your code ever runs, and whatever object your action returns is automatically serialized back into JSON for the HTTP response — you rarely call JsonSerializer directly in a typical controller because the framework does it for you, but understanding that this serialize/deserialize round trip is happening under the hood explains behaviors like property naming policies, ignored/renamed fields via attributes, and why a mismatched JSON shape produces a deserialization error or unexpected default values instead of an exception in some configurations.

codeExample.explanation: Serialize flattens the live Student object into JSON text; Deserialize<T> reconstructs an equivalent Student instance from that text.

mistakes: Assuming private fields/properties are serialized by default -- System.Text.Json serializes public readable properties by default, not private fields.
Forgetting a parameterless constructor or appropriate attributes when deserializing types with complex constructors, causing deserialization failures.
Not handling property name casing mismatches (PascalCase in C# vs camelCase JSON convention) without configuring JsonSerializerOptions.
Using binary serialization (BinaryFormatter) in new code -- it's obsolete/removed in modern .NET due to serious security vulnerabilities.
Serializing an object with circular references without configuring how to handle them, causing an exception or infinite recursion depending on the serializer.

followUps.question: Does ASP.NET Core call JsonSerializer directly in a typical controller?
followUps.answer: Usually not explicitly -- ASP.NET Core's model binding and formatters handle serialization/deserialization automatically for request bodies and action return values, using System.Text.Json by default. You'd call JsonSerializer directly for manual scenarios like caching a serialized object or building a custom middleware.

followUps.question: How do you control property naming (camelCase vs PascalCase) during serialization?
followUps.answer: Pass JsonSerializerOptions with PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase to Serialize/Deserialize, or configure it globally in ASP.NET Core's AddJsonOptions -- by default System.Text.Json is case-insensitive on deserialize but preserves C# property casing on serialize unless configured otherwise.

followUps.question: Why was BinaryFormatter deprecated?
followUps.answer: It allowed deserializing arbitrary types based on data in the payload itself, which enabled remote code execution attacks if an application deserialized untrusted binary data -- it's obsolete and disabled by default in modern .NET; JSON-based serialization with explicit target types is the safer alternative.

memoryHack.oneLiner: Serialize = flat-pack the furniture for shipping; Deserialize = assemble it back at the destination.
memoryHack.mnemonic: SD: Serialize-Down to text, Deserialize back up to an object.
memoryHack.memoryPalace: Picture a warehouse: a live, assembled sofa (an object) gets disassembled into flat-packed boxes labeled with instructions (JSON text) for shipping, and at the destination someone reads the instructions and reassembles the exact same sofa (deserialization).

bestPractices: Prefer System.Text.Json over older serializers (Newtonsoft.Json, BinaryFormatter) for new .NET projects unless a specific feature requires otherwise.
Use DTOs/models dedicated to the API contract rather than serializing internal domain entities directly, to avoid leaking internal implementation details.
Configure JsonSerializerOptions consistently (naming policy, null handling) across an application rather than ad hoc per call.
Never use BinaryFormatter for untrusted data -- it's a known remote code execution vector and disabled by default in modern .NET.
Validate deserialized objects before trusting them, since deserialization alone doesn't guarantee business-rule validity.
performanceTips: System.Text.Json is generally faster and more memory-efficient than the older Newtonsoft.Json for most workloads, especially with source-generated serializers (System.Text.Json source generation) for AOT/trimming-friendly, allocation-reduced serialization.
Avoid repeatedly serializing/deserializing large object graphs in hot paths -- cache serialized representations when the underlying data doesn't change frequently.
Streaming APIs (SerializeAsync/DeserializeAsync) avoid buffering an entire large payload in memory at once.

quiz.question: What does JsonSerializer.Serialize(obj) produce?
options: A JSON string representing the object's data
quiz.explanation: Serialize converts the in-memory object into a JSON-formatted string representation of its public property values.

quiz.question: In a typical ASP.NET Core Web API, when does an incoming JSON request body get deserialized?
options: Automatically via model binding, before the controller action runs
Only if you explicitly call JsonSerializer.Deserialize
Never -- APIs work directly with raw JSON strings
quiz.explanation: ASP.NET Core's model binding automatically deserializes the request body into the action's parameter type before your code executes.

quiz.question: Why is BinaryFormatter discouraged in modern .NET?
options: It has known remote code execution vulnerabilities when deserializing untrusted data
quiz.explanation: BinaryFormatter can be exploited to execute arbitrary code from crafted payloads, so it's considered unsafe and is obsolete/disabled by default.

flashcards.back: Converting an in-memory object into a transferable/storable format like JSON, XML, or binary.
Reconstructing an object from a serialized format back into memory.

flashcards.front: What's the modern default JSON serializer in .NET?
flashcards.back: System.Text.Json (JsonSerializer.Serialize / Deserialize<T>).

flashcards.front: Where does this happen automatically in Web APIs?
flashcards.back: ASP.NET Core model binding deserializes request bodies and serializes action return values automatically.
Known remote code execution risk when deserializing untrusted data -- obsolete/disabled in modern .NET.

revision30: Serialization converts a live object to a transferable format (JSON/XML/binary); deserialization converts it back. JsonSerializer.Serialize/Deserialize<T> are the standard .NET tools. Every Web API does this automatically for request/response bodies.
revision2min: Serialization takes a live in-memory object and converts it into a format suitable for transmission or storage, most commonly JSON in modern .NET, though XML and binary formats exist for other scenarios. Deserialization reverses this, parsing that transferable representation back into an equivalent in-memory object. The standard modern tool is System.Text.Json: JsonSerializer.Serialize(obj) turns an object into a JSON string of its public properties, and JsonSerializer.Deserialize<T>(json) parses JSON text back into a strongly-typed instance. This exact round trip happens automatically and invisibly in every ASP.NET Core Web API -- incoming request bodies are deserialized into your controller action's parameter type via model binding before your code runs, and whatever object your action returns is serialized into the JSON response body sent back to the client, so most application code never calls JsonSerializer directly despite depending on it constantly. Practical gotchas include property naming mismatches (PascalCase C# properties vs camelCase JSON convention, configurable via JsonSerializerOptions), the fact that only public readable properties are serialized by default (not private fields), and the security risk of legacy binary serializers like BinaryFormatter, which can be exploited for remote code execution on untrusted input and are obsolete in modern .NET in favor of explicitly-typed JSON deserialization.

title: var vs dynamic
interviewQuestion: What's the difference between var and dynamic in C#?

story.setup: Two assistants are handed unlabeled boxes and asked to describe their contents.
scenes: The first assistant, var, opens the box IMMEDIATELY at the moment it's handed over, reads a permanent label off the contents, and writes that exact label on the box forever — var x = 10; and the box is now permanently 'int', full stop, checked and locked in before anyone ever touches it again.

The second assistant, dynamic, doesn't look inside at all — dynamic z = "abc"; the box is left unlabeled, and every time someone asks it to do something, it waits until that exact moment to peek inside and hope the contents can do what's asked.
z.Foo(); compiles instantly because the dynamic assistant never checks in advance — but the moment the box is actually opened at runtime and there's no Foo method on a string, it crashes right there.

var never allows the box's declared label to change even if the value is replaced later — but dynamic can be reassigned to a completely different kind of content at any point, since it was never labeled to begin with.
story.moral: var is compile-time type inference — the compiler determines and locks in the exact type immediately; dynamic defers all type checking to runtime, trading compile-time safety for flexibility.

analogy: var is an assistant who reads the label the instant the box arrives and locks it in forever; dynamic is an assistant who never checks the box's contents until the exact moment someone asks it to do something.
explanation: var lets the compiler infer a variable's exact static type at compile time from the initializer expression — once inferred, that type is fixed for the variable's lifetime, exactly as if you'd written the type explicitly; it still gets full compile-time type checking and IntelliSense. dynamic defers type resolution entirely to runtime — the compiler performs no type checking on member access at all, and any member call is only resolved (and can only fail) when that line actually executes, via the Dynamic Language Runtime. A dynamic variable's underlying type can also change across reassignments, unlike var. In practice, var should be used routinely for readability wherever the type is obvious from context; dynamic should be reserved for narrow scenarios like COM interop, working with genuinely unknown-shape JSON, or heavy reflection-based code, since it sacrifices compile-time safety and IDE tooling support.
interviewAnswerShort: var is compile-time type inference — the compiler determines and locks in a fixed type immediately, with full compile-time checking; dynamic skips all compile-time type checking and resolves member access at runtime, so type errors surface as runtime exceptions instead of build failures.
interviewAnswerDetailed: var is purely a compile-time convenience: `var x = 10;` tells the compiler to infer the variable's type from the right-hand side, and the compiler substitutes int in that exact spot at compile time — after that, x is an int for its entire scope, gets full static type checking, IntelliSense, and refactoring support, exactly as if you'd written `int x = 10;` explicitly; var carries zero runtime overhead or behavior difference from an explicitly-typed variable. dynamic is fundamentally different: `dynamic z = "abc";` tells the compiler to skip static type checking on z entirely and instead resolve any member access, method call, or operation against z at runtime, via the Dynamic Language Runtime (DLR); `z.Foo();` compiles successfully even though string has no Foo method, because the compiler makes no attempt to verify it — the failure (a RuntimeBinderException) only occurs when that line actually executes and the DLR discovers there's no matching member. A dynamic variable's underlying value — and effectively its type — can also be freely reassigned to a completely different type across its lifetime, which var does not allow since var's inferred type is fixed once and for all at the point of declaration. Because dynamic trades away compile-time safety, IntelliSense, and most refactoring tool support, it should be used sparingly and deliberately: legitimate use cases include COM interop (where member signatures aren't statically known to C#), working with genuinely unknown or highly variable JSON/XML shapes where defining a static type isn't practical, and reflection-heavy or dynamically-generated-type scenarios. For everyday code, var should be used freely wherever the inferred type is obvious from the initializer, purely as a readability aid — it is not, and never was, a way to opt out of static typing.

codeExample.code:
var x = 10; // int forever, resolved at compile time

dynamic z = "abc";
z.Foo(); // COMPILES -- crashes at runtime (RuntimeBinderException)

dynamic reassignable = 5;   // starts as int
reassignable = "now a string"; // legal -- dynamic can change underlying type
codeExample.explanation: var's type is fixed and checked at compile time; dynamic skips compile-time checking entirely, allowing invalid member calls to compile and fail only at runtime, and permitting type changes across reassignments.

mistakes: Believing var makes a variable's type flexible or 'weakly typed' -- it's fully statically typed, just inferred rather than explicitly written.
Using dynamic as a general substitute for proper typing or generics, losing compile-time safety for no real benefit.
Expecting dynamic member-access errors to be caught by the compiler -- they only surface as exceptions at runtime.
Overusing dynamic in performance-sensitive code -- every dynamic operation goes through the DLR's runtime binding, which has real overhead compared to statically-resolved calls.
Assuming var and dynamic are interchangeable because both omit an explicit type name in the declaration.

followUps.question: Does var work without an initializer, like var x;?
followUps.answer: No -- the compiler needs the initializer expression to infer the type, so var x; without an initializer is a compile error. dynamic z; is legal without immediate initialization since its type is deferred to runtime regardless.

followUps.question: What exception is thrown when a dynamic member call fails at runtime?
followUps.answer: A Microsoft.CSharp.RuntimeBinder.RuntimeBinderException, thrown by the DLR when it can't find a matching member/operation on the runtime type of the dynamic value.

followUps.question: Is there a performance cost to using dynamic?
followUps.answer: Yes -- every operation on a dynamic value goes through the DLR's call-site caching and runtime binding machinery instead of a directly resolved, potentially inlined static method call, making dynamic operations measurably slower than their statically-typed equivalents, especially in hot loops.

memoryHack.oneLiner: var reads and locks the label instantly; dynamic never checks the box until the moment it's used.
memoryHack.mnemonic: VC-DR: Var = Compile-time; Dynamic = Runtime.
memoryHack.memoryPalace: Picture two assistants: one labels a box the instant it arrives and never touches it again (var), the other carries an unlabeled box everywhere and only peeks inside the exact moment someone asks it to do something with it (dynamic).

bestPractices: Use var freely for local variables whenever the type is obvious from the right-hand side, purely for readability.
Reserve dynamic for narrow, justified cases -- COM interop, genuinely unknown-shape data, or reflection-heavy scenarios.
Prefer strongly-typed models (records/classes) or JsonDocument/JsonElement over dynamic for parsing JSON of a known or mostly-known shape.
Add explicit null/member checks around dynamic usage since the compiler provides no safety net there.
Avoid dynamic in hot paths or performance-critical code due to DLR call-site overhead.
performanceTips: dynamic operations incur real runtime overhead from DLR binding and call-site caching -- avoid in tight loops.
var itself has zero runtime cost or behavior difference versus writing the explicit type -- it's purely a compile-time inference convenience.
Repeated dynamic calls on the same call site do get cached by the DLR after the first resolution, reducing but not eliminating the overhead on subsequent calls.

quiz.question: When is a var variable's type determined?
options: At compile time, from the initializer expression
It's determined by the garbage collector
It changes dynamically as the program runs
quiz.explanation: var is purely compile-time type inference; once inferred, the type is fixed and behaves exactly like an explicitly-typed variable.

quiz.question: What happens when you call a non-existent method on a dynamic variable?
options: It compiles successfully and throws a RuntimeBinderException at runtime
It automatically converts to the correct type
quiz.explanation: dynamic skips compile-time member checking entirely; invalid member access only fails when the DLR attempts to resolve it at runtime.

quiz.question: Which scenario is a legitimate use case for dynamic?
options: COM interop or working with genuinely unknown-shape data
Avoiding writing explicit types in normal business logic
quiz.explanation: dynamic is intended for scenarios like COM interop, reflection-heavy code, or unpredictable data shapes, where static typing genuinely isn't practical.

flashcards.back: Compile time -- inferred from the initializer, then fixed permanently.
Runtime -- via the Dynamic Language Runtime (DLR), on every member access.
Yes -- full static checking, exactly like an explicitly-typed variable.
No -- invalid member calls compile fine and throw RuntimeBinderException at runtime.

flashcards.back: COM interop, and working with genuinely unknown-shape JSON/reflection-heavy code.

summary: var infers and locks a variable's type at compile time with full static checking and zero overhead; dynamic defers all type resolution to runtime via the DLR, trading compile-time safety for flexibility at a real performance cost.

title: Compile Time vs Runtime
interviewQuestion: What's the difference between compile time and runtime in C#, and which errors get caught at each stage?

story.setup: A theater production has two completely separate stages of scrutiny: the script read-through, and the live performance in front of an audience.
scenes: During the script read-through (compile time), the director catches every typo, every character with mismatched dialogue, every scene that structurally doesn't make sense — int x = "hello"; is a line so wrong the read-through refuses to even continue.

The read-through also decides, in advance, which of several actors with the same name plays which scene based on the script's stage directions — that's overload resolution, settled before the curtain ever rises.

Once the curtain goes up (runtime), new problems can surface that no read-through could catch — an actor forgets their line entirely (a NullReferenceException), or the math for a prop malfunctions live on stage (10 / 0 builds fine, crashes at runtime).

During the live show, the actual understudy who steps in depends on who's really wearing the costume that night — that's overriding, resolved dynamically based on the real object at runtime, not decided in advance like overload resolution was.
Pressing F5 is the whole night: the read-through happens first (compile), and only if it passes does the curtain rise for the actual performance (run).
story.moral: Compile time catches structural and type errors before anything runs and resolves overloads; runtime is when the program actually executes, throws logic errors like NullReferenceException, and resolves overrides dynamically.

analogy: Compile time is the theater's script read-through catching typos and mismatched dialogue before curtain-up; runtime is the live performance where an actor can still forget a line in front of the audience.
explanation: Compile time is when you build your code — the C# compiler translates source into Intermediate Language (IL) and catches syntax errors, type errors, and resolves method overloading (choosing the correct overload based on the compile-time types of the arguments). Runtime is when the compiled program actually executes — this is when a NullReferenceException or DivideByZeroException can occur, when method overriding is resolved (the actual method invoked depends on the object's real runtime type via virtual dispatch), and when dependency injection and garbage collection do their work. `int x = "hello";` fails to build because it's a compile-time type mismatch, while `int c = 10 / 0;` builds successfully but throws at runtime because integer division by a constant zero is only caught by some compilers as a warning, and by a non-constant zero divisor it's purely a runtime failure. var is resolved at compile time; dynamic defers to runtime. const is a compile-time value; readonly is resolved at runtime. Pressing F5 in an IDE performs both stages in sequence — it compiles first, and only runs if that succeeds.
interviewAnswerShort: Compile time is when the compiler translates your source to IL and catches syntax/type errors and resolves overloads; runtime is when the program actually executes, where things like NullReferenceException occur and method overriding is resolved dynamically.
interviewAnswerDetailed: Compile time refers to the phase where the C# compiler (Roslyn) processes your source code, checks it for syntactic correctness and static type correctness, and translates it into Intermediate Language (IL) plus metadata bundled into an assembly. Errors caught at this stage include type mismatches like `int x = "hello";`, undeclared variables, missing semicolons, and inaccessible members — none of these ever reach a running program because the build simply fails first. Compile time is also when method overload resolution happens: if a class has multiple methods named Process with different parameter types, the compiler determines which specific overload a given call site invokes based on the compile-time (static) types of the arguments, and that choice is baked into the emitted IL — it does not change based on what happens at runtime. Runtime refers to the phase after a successful build, when the CLR actually loads and executes that IL — this is when logic errors surface that the compiler cannot statically detect, such as NullReferenceException (dereferencing a null reference that only turns out to be null given specific program state) or `int c = 10 / 0;`, which — when the divisor is a genuine runtime value rather than the literal constant 0 — builds fine and throws a DivideByZeroException only when that line actually executes. Runtime is also when method overriding is resolved: unlike overload resolution, which is fixed at compile time based on static types, overriding is resolved dynamically via virtual dispatch based on the object's actual runtime type, which is why polymorphism works even though the compile-time reference type might be a base class. Runtime is additionally when dependency injection containers resolve concrete implementations, and when the garbage collector reclaims memory — none of which the compiler is involved in. The var/dynamic and const/readonly pairs are a clean mnemonic pair for this distinction: var and const are resolved at compile time, while dynamic and readonly are resolved at runtime. Practically, pressing F5 (or dotnet run) performs both stages back to back — the compile step runs first, and the program is only executed if compilation succeeds; a compile-time error means the program never runs at all, whereas a runtime error means the program started but failed partway through.

codeExample.explanation: A genuine type mismatch fails to build entirely, while a runtime-dependent value like a variable divisor compiles fine and can only fail once the program actually executes.

mistakes: Confusing overload resolution (compile-time, based on static argument types) with overriding (runtime, based on the object's actual type).

Assuming all division-by-zero errors are caught at compile time -- only a literal constant zero divisor is typically flagged, and even then not always as a hard error; a runtime-computed zero divisor always throws only at runtime.
Believing var means 'runtime-determined type' -- it's resolved entirely at compile time, unlike dynamic.
Forgetting that a successful build guarantees no syntax/type errors, but guarantees nothing about runtime correctness (nulls, logic bugs, exceptions).
Thinking readonly fields are known at compile time like const -- they're resolved at runtime, during construction.

followUps.question: Give the const/readonly and var/dynamic pairing as a memory aid -- which pair belongs where?
followUps.answer: Compile time: Overloading, var, const. Runtime: Overriding, dynamic, readonly. Pressing F5 does both -- compile, then run.

followUps.question: Can a program with zero compile-time errors still fail?
followUps.answer: Yes -- a clean build only guarantees syntactic and static type correctness. Logic errors, null references, division by a runtime-computed zero, unhandled exceptions, and incorrect business logic are all runtime concerns the compiler cannot detect.

followUps.question: Why does overload resolution happening at compile time matter for polymorphism?
followUps.answer: Because it means which overload is called is fixed by the STATIC (declared) type of the argument, not its runtime type -- this is why calling an overloaded method with a base-class-typed reference to a derived object picks the base-class overload, unlike overriding, which always dispatches to the derived implementation based on the actual runtime type.

memoryHack.oneLiner: Compile time = the script read-through; runtime = the live performance in front of an audience.
memoryHack.mnemonic: COV-RID: Compile=Overload,var; Runtime=oveRriding,dynamic,readonly.
memoryHack.memoryPalace: Picture a theater: backstage read-through catching every typo before curtain-up (compile time, overload resolution, var, const) versus the live show where an actor can still forget a line in front of an audience (runtime, overriding, dynamic, readonly).

bestPractices: Lean on the compiler as your first line of defense -- prefer explicit, strongly-typed code that surfaces mistakes at compile time rather than runtime.
Add null checks and guard clauses for values whose null-ness the compiler can't fully guarantee, even with nullable reference types enabled.
Use nullable reference types (C# 8+) to shift more null-related bugs from runtime exceptions to compile-time warnings.
Write unit tests specifically to catch runtime-only logic errors that a successful build can never guarantee away.
Understand overload vs override resolution when debugging unexpected method dispatch -- they follow completely different resolution timing and rules.
performanceTips: Compile-time resolved calls (non-virtual methods, overload resolution) can be more aggressively inlined and optimized by the JIT than runtime-dispatched virtual calls.
Nullable reference type annotations have zero runtime cost -- they're purely a compile-time analysis feature.
Catching errors at compile time is effectively free compared to the cost of a runtime exception, which involves stack unwinding and exception object allocation.

quiz.question: At which stage is method overload resolution decided?
options: Runtime, based on the object's actual type
Compile time, based on the static types of the arguments
It's decided by the garbage collector
quiz.explanation: Overload resolution is fixed by the compiler based on the compile-time (static) types of the arguments at the call site.

options: The compiler can't detect any division at all
A literal constant zero divisor can be flagged by the compiler, but a value only known at runtime can't be checked until execution
quiz.explanation: The compiler can sometimes catch a literal constant division by zero, but a divisor computed from runtime input is only checkable when the program actually executes.

options: Overriding is compile-time, var is runtime

const and readonly are both compile-time
quiz.explanation: Overloading and const are resolved at compile time; overriding and readonly are resolved at runtime.

The program executes; NullReferenceException etc. can occur; overriding resolved dynamically; DI and GC run.

revision2min: Compile time is when the C# compiler translates your source code into IL and metadata, catching every syntax error and static type mismatch before the program ever runs -- code like `int x = "hello";` simply fails to build. This is also when method overload resolution is fixed: the compiler picks which overload a call invokes based on the compile-time (static) types of the arguments, and that decision is baked permanently into the emitted IL. Runtime is the subsequent phase where the CLR actually executes that compiled IL, and it's when logic errors the compiler couldn't statically detect finally surface -- a NullReferenceException from dereferencing an unexpectedly-null reference, or a DivideByZeroException from a runtime-computed zero divisor (`int c = 10 / divisor;` builds fine regardless of divisor's eventual value).
