title: Stack vs Heap and Heap Allocation
interviewQuestion: What is heap allocation? Explain the difference between the stack and the heap.

story.setup: A restaurant has a fast, personal notepad at every waiter's station, and a large shared walk-in storage room out back.
scenes: Each waiter keeps a small personal notepad at their own station — orders scribbled there (int x = 5;) are instant to write and instant to throw away the moment the waiter's shift note is done. That's the stack: fast, small, automatic, freed the moment the scope ends.

For a big catering order (Person p = new Person();), the waiter can't fit the whole thing on their notepad — they walk it back to the shared walk-in storage room (the heap) and just leave a sticky note on their pad with the storage room's shelf number.

The sticky note itself (the reference) lives on the fast notepad, but the actual catering order (the object) sits in the shared storage room, managed and eventually cleaned out by the kitchen's cleanup crew (the GC) — not automatically freed the instant the waiter's shift ends.

A waiter who keeps walking to the storage room for every tiny order (boxing a value type, or concatenating strings in a loop) slows the whole kitchen down — trips to the shared room are inherently slower than scribbling on your own notepad, and every trip adds cleanup work for the crew later.
story.moral: The stack is fast, automatic, per-call memory for value-type locals and references; the heap is larger, GC-managed memory for every reference-type object — heap allocation is slower and creates cleanup work, which is exactly why boxing and loop concatenation hurt performance.

analogy: The stack is a waiter's personal notepad — fast, small, automatically cleared each shift; the heap is the shared walk-in storage room — larger, but needs the kitchen's cleanup crew (the GC) to eventually clear it.
explanation: The stack is a fast, small, automatically-managed region of memory used for value-type local variables and for the references (addresses) that reference-type variables hold; memory on the stack is freed the instant the method that owns it returns, with essentially zero overhead. The heap is a larger, garbage-collector-managed region where every object created with new for a reference type actually lives — `int x = 5;` stores its value directly on the stack, while `Person p = new Person();` stores the reference p on the stack but allocates the actual Person object on the heap. Heap allocation is inherently slower than stack allocation and creates work for the garbage collector, which is exactly why patterns that cause excessive heap allocation — boxing value types, concatenating strings in a loop instead of using StringBuilder, or creating many short-lived objects in a hot path — measurably hurt performance through both the allocation cost itself and the resulting GC pressure.
interviewAnswerShort: The stack is fast, automatically-managed memory for value-type locals and references, freed the instant a method returns; the heap is larger, GC-managed memory where every reference-type object actually lives — heap allocation is slower and creates GC work, which is why boxing and loop string concatenation hurt performance.
interviewAnswerDetailed: The stack is a region of memory organized as a simple last-in-first-out structure, one per thread, used to store value-type local variables directly and to store the reference (address) portion of reference-type local variables. Allocating on the stack is extremely cheap — it's essentially just moving a stack pointer — and deallocation is equally cheap and fully deterministic: the moment a method returns, its entire stack frame, including everything declared as a local within it, is simply popped and reclaimed instantly, with no garbage collector involvement at all. The heap, by contrast, is a much larger pool of memory managed by the .NET garbage collector, and it's where the actual data for every reference-type instance lives — when you write `Person p = new Person();`, the variable p itself (a reference/address) sits on the stack, but the Person object's actual field data is allocated on the heap; that heap allocation persists independently of any single method's stack frame, and is only reclaimed later by the GC once nothing reachable still references it. This distinction directly explains several classic performance patterns: heap allocation involves more bookkeeping than a stack push (finding free space, potentially triggering a collection) and, critically, creates a live object the GC must eventually track and collect, generating collection pressure — a struct-heavy, allocation-light hot path stays almost entirely on the fast stack, while patterns like boxing a value type into object (an implicit heap allocation), building up a string with += inside a loop (each iteration allocates a brand-new heap string), or creating many short-lived class instances inside a tight loop, all generate substantial avoidable heap traffic and correspondingly avoidable GC work, which is precisely why those patterns are flagged as performance anti-patterns elsewhere in C#.

codeExample.code:
int x = 5;             // stack
Person p = new Person(); // reference on stack, OBJECT on heap

// Heap-allocation-heavy anti-patterns:
object boxed = x;                     // boxing -- heap allocation
string s = ""; for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) s += i; // 1000 heap allocations
codeExample.explanation: A local int lives entirely on the stack; a Person object's data lives on the heap even though its reference sits on the stack; boxing and loop concatenation both create unnecessary heap allocations and GC pressure.

mistakes: Assuming all value types always live on the stack -- a value-type field inside a class instance lives on the heap as part of that object.
Believing heap-allocated objects are freed the instant their referencing method returns -- they persist until the GC determines nothing reachable references them anymore.
Underestimating the cumulative cost of many small heap allocations (boxing, loop string concatenation) in hot code paths.
Assuming the stack is unlimited -- deep recursion can exhaust the stack and throw a StackOverflowException, which cannot be caught.

Thinking arrays of value types are stored value-by-value on the stack -- arrays are reference types, so even an int[] array's elements live on the heap, contiguously, with only the array reference on the stack.

followUps.question: Is a struct always allocated on the stack?
followUps.answer: No -- a struct lives wherever it's declared. A local struct variable is on the stack, but a struct that's a field of a class instance, or an element of an array (a reference type), lives on the heap as part of that containing object.

followUps.question: Why does heap allocation hurt performance specifically?
followUps.answer: It's slower than a stack push due to allocation bookkeeping, and more importantly it creates GC-tracked garbage -- every heap allocation is potential future GC work. This is exactly why boxing and string concatenation in loops hurt performance: each one is an avoidable heap allocation.

followUps.question: What happens if the stack runs out of space?
followUps.answer: A StackOverflowException is thrown -- typically from unbounded or excessively deep recursion. Unlike most exceptions, it cannot be caught with try/catch in managed code and terminates the process, because the stack itself, needed to even run exception-handling code, is exhausted.

memoryHack.oneLiner: Stack = your own fast notepad, cleared automatically; Heap = the shared storage room, cleaned up later by the crew.
memoryHack.mnemonic: SHAG: Stack=fast/auto, Heap=big/GC.
memoryHack.memoryPalace: Picture a restaurant: a waiter's personal notepad cleared instantly at shift's end (stack) beside a shared walk-in storage room that needs a cleanup crew to eventually clear out abandoned orders (heap, managed by the GC).

bestPractices: Favor small, immutable structs for hot-path, allocation-sensitive code to keep data on the stack.
Avoid boxing and loop-based string concatenation in performance-critical paths -- both cause avoidable heap allocations.
Be cautious with deep or unbounded recursion, which can exhaust the stack and crash the process with an unrecoverable StackOverflowException.
Use object pooling or Span<T>/stackalloc for extremely allocation-sensitive scenarios (high-throughput services, game loops).
Profile allocations with a memory profiler before hand-optimizing -- premature stack/heap micro-optimization often isn't worth the complexity.
performanceTips: Stack allocation/deallocation is essentially free; heap allocation has real cost plus downstream GC cost.
Reducing heap allocations in hot loops (avoiding boxing, avoiding LINQ's iterator allocations in extreme hot paths, using StringBuilder) reduces GC pause frequency and duration.
Span<T> and stackalloc allow genuinely stack-based buffers for high-performance code, avoiding heap allocation entirely for temporary data.

quiz.question: Where does the actual data of `Person p = new Person();` live?
options: The reference p is on the stack; the Person object's data is on the heap
Entirely on the heap, including the reference
It depends on the CPU architecture
quiz.explanation: The variable p holds a reference stored on the stack, but the Person object it points to is allocated on the heap.

quiz.question: Why is heap allocation generally slower and more costly than stack allocation?
options: It isn't -- they're identical in cost
It requires more bookkeeping and creates objects the GC must eventually track and collect
The heap uses a different CPU
Heap allocation always requires disk I/O
quiz.explanation: Heap allocation involves more overhead to find and reserve space, and produces GC-tracked garbage that must eventually be collected, unlike the near-free push/pop of the stack.

quiz.question: What happens on deep, unbounded recursion?
options: The heap runs out of memory first
A StackOverflowException is thrown, which cannot be caught
The GC automatically increases stack size
Nothing -- recursion is unlimited in C#
quiz.explanation: Each recursive call adds a new stack frame; exceeding the stack's fixed size throws an uncatchable StackOverflowException that terminates the process.

flashcards.back: Value-type locals, and the references (addresses) of reference-type locals -- freed automatically on method return.
The actual data of every reference-type object created with new -- managed and eventually reclaimed by the GC.

flashcards.front: Is stack or heap allocation faster?
flashcards.back: Stack -- essentially a pointer move; heap involves more bookkeeping plus future GC work.

flashcards.front: Why do boxing and loop string concatenation hurt performance?
flashcards.back: Both cause unnecessary heap allocations, creating avoidable GC pressure.

flashcards.front: What happens when the stack is exhausted?
flashcards.back: An uncatchable StackOverflowException, typically from deep/unbounded recursion, terminating the process.

revision30: Stack: fast, small, automatic -- value-type locals and references, freed on method return. Heap: large, GC-managed -- every reference-type object's actual data. Heap allocation is slower and creates GC work, which is why boxing and loop string concatenation hurt performance.
revision2min: The stack is a fast, per-thread, last-in-first-out memory region holding value-type local variables directly and the reference portion of reference-type locals; allocating and freeing stack memory is essentially free, since a method's entire stack frame is simply popped the instant it returns, with zero GC involvement. The heap is a much larger pool managed by the garbage collector, and it's where the actual data of every reference-type instance created with new truly lives -- `Person p = new Person();` puts the reference p on the stack but allocates the Person object's fields on the heap, and that allocation persists independently of any single method call until the GC determines nothing reachable still references it. This distinction directly explains several well-known performance anti-patterns: heap allocation carries more overhead than a stack push and, more importantly, produces GC-tracked garbage the collector must eventually process, so patterns like boxing a value type into object, or concatenating strings with += inside a loop (each iteration allocating a brand-new heap string), generate avoidable heap traffic and GC pressure -- exactly why both are flagged elsewhere as performance concerns. It's worth remembering that value types don't always live on the stack -- a struct field inside a class instance, or a struct element in an array, is stored on the heap as part of that containing object, since a value type simply lives wherever it's declared. Deep or unbounded recursion can also exhaust the stack's fixed size, throwing an uncatchable StackOverflowException that terminates the process immediately, since the stack space needed to even run exception-handling logic is itself gone.

summary: The stack offers fast, automatic memory for locals and references, while the heap holds every reference-type object's actual data under GC management — heap allocation's extra cost and GC pressure is the root cause behind performance anti-patterns like boxing and loop string concatenation.

title: IL, JIT and CLR
interviewQuestion: What are IL, JIT, and CLR, and how do they fit together in the .NET execution model?

story.setup: A global publishing house writes every book in one universal shorthand, then has local translators convert it to the reader's native language only the moment someone actually opens the book.
scenes: Whether the author writes in C#, VB.NET, or F#, every manuscript is converted into the SAME universal shorthand (IL) before it's shipped — no matter which language you wrote in, the shipped .dll speaks one common tongue.

The shorthand isn't readable by any reader directly — it needs a local translator (the JIT compiler) stationed at every regional office, who converts each chapter into the reader's native tongue (native machine code) right as they're about to read it, one method at a time.

The whole operation — hiring translators, managing the shelf of books, enforcing that every book obeys universal content rules (type safety), handling misprinted pages (exceptions) — is run by one head office: the CLR, the Common Language Runtime.

Because the shorthand is universal, the SAME shipped manuscript works whether the reader is in an x64 city or an ARM city, Windows or Linux — you ship once, and each regional office's own translator tailors it to local needs.
story.moral: IL is the language-independent, half-compiled format every .NET language compiles to; the JIT translates it to native machine code per-method at runtime; the CLR is the whole execution engine that hosts, manages, and secures that process.

analogy: IL is a universal publishing shorthand every author's language compiles into; the JIT is the local translator who converts each chapter to native language only the moment someone reads it; the CLR is the head office running the whole operation.
explanation: IL (Intermediate Language, also called MSIL or CIL) is the half-compiled code that lives inside your .dll — the C# compiler translates your source into IL plus metadata, but IL is not native machine code and cannot run directly on the CPU. JIT (Just-In-Time compiler) converts that IL into native machine code at runtime, on a per-method basis, the first time each method is actually called. CLR (Common Language Runtime) is the overall .NET execution engine that hosts this whole pipeline: memory management and garbage collection, JIT compilation, type safety enforcement via the Common Type System (CTS), exception handling, IL verification and security, thread management, and cross-language interop — C#, VB.NET, and F# all compile down to the same IL, which is precisely why the runtime is called "Common." IL exists to provide both language independence (many source languages compile to one IL) and platform independence (one IL, and the JIT emits the appropriate native code for whichever CPU architecture and OS it's actually running on) — you ship a single .dll, and each machine's CLR tailors it locally. Ahead-of-time alternatives like NGen, ReadyToRun, and Native AOT pre-compile some or all of that native code before runtime specifically to remove JIT warm-up cost.
interviewAnswerShort: The C# compiler translates source code into IL (Intermediate Language) inside your .dll; the JIT compiles that IL into native machine code per method at runtime; the CLR is the overall .NET execution engine hosting memory management, JIT compilation, type safety, and exception handling around that whole process.
interviewAnswerDetailed: When you build a C# project, the compiler doesn't produce native machine code directly — it produces Intermediate Language (IL, also called MSIL or CIL), a CPU-independent, half-compiled instruction set, plus metadata describing your types, stored inside your assembly (.dll or .exe). IL alone cannot execute directly on a CPU; it needs the Just-In-Time (JIT) compiler, a component of the CLR, to translate it into real native machine code — critically, this happens per method and lazily, the first time each method is actually invoked, rather than compiling the entire assembly upfront, which is why it's called 'just in time' rather than ahead of time. The Common Language Runtime (CLR) is the overarching execution engine that hosts this entire pipeline and provides a broad set of services beyond just JIT compilation: automatic memory management and garbage collection, enforcement of type safety through the Common Type System (CTS) — which is what guarantees a string in C# and a String in VB.NET are genuinely the same type at the runtime level — structured exception handling, IL verification for security (ensuring loaded code doesn't perform illegal memory operations), thread management, and interop across the many languages that target it. The reason it's called 'Common' is that C#, VB.NET, F#, and other .NET languages all compile down to the exact same IL and run on the exact same CLR — a class written in F# can be consumed seamlessly by C# code because, at the IL level, there's no distinction between them. IL's design serves two goals simultaneously: language independence, since many different source languages funnel into one common intermediate format, and platform independence, since a single compiled IL assembly can be JIT-compiled into the correct native code for whatever CPU architecture (x64, ARM) and OS (Windows, Linux, macOS) it happens to be running on — you genuinely ship one .dll, and each machine's own CLR produces the native code appropriate to it. Because JIT compilation happens lazily and has a real (if usually small) per-method compilation cost the first time each method runs, .NET also offers ahead-of-time compilation alternatives for scenarios where that warm-up cost matters: NGen (legacy), ReadyToRun (pre-JITs common paths while still shipping IL as a fallback), and Native AOT (compiles the entire application to native code ahead of time, eliminating the JIT and CLR-hosting overhead entirely for fast cold-start scenarios like serverless functions).

mistakes: Believing C# compiles directly to native machine code -- it compiles to IL, which the JIT then translates to native code at runtime.
Confusing the JIT with the CLR -- JIT compilation is one specific service the CLR provides, not the entirety of what the CLR does.
Assuming JIT compilation happens once for the whole assembly upfront -- it happens per method, lazily, the first time each method is invoked.
Thinking IL is human-readable machine code -- it's a distinct, CPU-independent instruction format that itself must still be compiled before execution.
Overlooking that ahead-of-time options (ReadyToRun, Native AOT) exist specifically to reduce or eliminate JIT warm-up cost for cold-start-sensitive scenarios.

followUps.question: What exactly does the CLR do, beyond JIT compilation?
followUps.answer: Memory management + GC, JIT compilation, type safety (CTS), exception handling, IL verification/security, thread management, and language interop -- C#, VB.NET and F# all compile to the same IL, hence 'Common'.

followUps.question: How does Native AOT differ from the standard JIT model?
followUps.answer: Native AOT compiles the entire application directly to native machine code ahead of time, at build/publish time, rather than shipping IL and relying on the JIT at runtime -- this eliminates JIT warm-up cost and reduces cold-start latency (valuable for serverless/CLI tools) at the cost of losing some runtime flexibility (like certain reflection-heavy or dynamic-codegen scenarios) and requiring platform-specific builds instead of one portable IL assembly.

memoryHack.oneLiner: IL = universal shorthand; JIT = local translator; CLR = the head office running it all.
memoryHack.mnemonic: ICJ: IL -> Compiled by JIT -> hosted by CLR.
memoryHack.memoryPalace: Picture a global publishing house: manuscripts in any author's language get converted to one universal shorthand (IL), a local translator converts each chapter to native language only when a reader opens it (JIT), and the head office runs the whole operation -- security, memory, exceptions (CLR).

bestPractices: Understand that a clean, portable IL assembly is the standard, most flexible deployment model -- reach for Native AOT/ReadyToRun only when cold-start latency genuinely matters.
Don't assume all .NET languages perform identically at runtime just because they share IL -- language-level differences in generated IL patterns can still matter for performance.
Use ReadyToRun for server apps wanting faster startup while retaining full JIT flexibility as a fallback.
Consider Native AOT for serverless functions, CLI tools, or containerized microservices where cold-start time is critical.
Remember CTS (Common Type System) is what makes cross-language interop safe -- don't design public APIs around language-specific type quirks that don't map cleanly across CTS.
performanceTips: JIT compilation has a real per-method first-call cost ("warm-up") -- long-running server apps amortize this quickly, but short-lived processes (CLI tools, serverless cold starts) feel it more.
ReadyToRun pre-JITs common code paths at publish time, reducing startup latency while still allowing full JIT for anything not pre-compiled.
Native AOT eliminates JIT entirely, giving the fastest possible cold start at the cost of some dynamic runtime flexibility and larger, platform-specific binaries.

Tiered compilation (enabled by default in modern .NET) lets the JIT quickly produce a fast-to-compile, less-optimized version of hot methods first, then recompile them with heavier optimization once they're proven genuinely hot.

title: Garbage Collection
interviewQuestion: Explain how garbage collection works in .NET, including generations.

story.setup: A hotel's housekeeping crew sweeps through every floor overnight, deciding which rooms are truly vacated and which still have a guest inside.
scenes: The crew starts at the front desk's active guest list (the roots — stack locals, statics, registers) and walks room to room from there, marking every room genuinely reachable from that list as still occupied — that's the Mark phase.

Every room NOT marked occupied gets swept clean and returned to available inventory — that's Sweep. Afterward, the crew slides the remaining occupied rooms together to close up gaps and avoid a fragmented, patchy floor plan — that's Compact.

New guests check into a fast-turnover wing (Gen 0) that gets swept almost every single night, since most guests only stay one night. A guest who's still there after several sweeps gets moved to a quieter wing (Gen 1), swept less often — and long-term residents eventually land in the permanent-suites wing (Gen 2: caches, singletons, statics), swept rarely, in an expensive, thorough inspection.

One VIP asks the manager to personally order an immediate, building-wide inspection right now — GC.Collect() — but that forces a full, disruptive stop-the-work sweep of every wing at once, which usually makes the hotel run WORSE, not better, and is reserved for diagnostics only.

A guest who left behind a physical room key (an unmanaged resource — file handle, DB connection) isn't handled by housekeeping at all — that's the GC's blind spot; only using + IDisposable reliably collects those.
story.moral: The GC finds unreachable objects by tracing from roots (Mark), reclaims them (Sweep), and defragments memory (Compact) — generational collection makes this cheap by sweeping short-lived objects constantly and long-lived objects rarely, but it only ever manages memory, never unmanaged resources.

analogy: Garbage collection is overnight hotel housekeeping — marking which rooms are still occupied by tracing from the front desk's active guest list, sweeping the rest clean, and periodically compacting the floor plan; frequent-turnover rooms get swept nightly, long-term suites almost never.
explanation: The GC automatically reclaims heap memory from objects no longer reachable from any root — stack locals, static fields, and CPU registers. It works in three phases: Mark, tracing from all roots and marking every object still reachable as alive; Sweep, reclaiming the memory of everything not marked; and Compact, sliding surviving objects together to close gaps and prevent fragmentation. Objects are organized into generations based on age: Gen 0 holds new objects and is collected very often and cheaply, since most objects die young; Gen 1 is a buffer of Gen 0 survivors, collected less often; Gen 2 holds long-lived objects like caches, singletons, and statics, and is collected rarely via the expensive full collection; a separate Large Object Heap (LOH) holds objects at least 85,000 bytes, is collected alongside Gen 2, and is not compacted by default. Objects that survive a collection in their current generation are promoted to the next one up. The GC only manages memory — it does not handle unmanaged resources like file handles, database connections, or sockets, which require IDisposable and using instead — and you should never call GC.Collect() manually, since it forces a disruptive full stop-the-world collection and usually makes performance worse; it exists for diagnostics and benchmarks only.
interviewAnswerShort: The GC traces reachability from roots (stack, statics, registers) in a Mark phase, reclaims unreachable memory in Sweep, and defragments in Compact; it uses generations (0, 1, 2, plus the Large Object Heap) so short-lived objects are collected cheaply and often while long-lived ones are collected rarely, and it manages memory only, never unmanaged resources.
interviewAnswerDetailed: The .NET garbage collector automatically reclaims heap memory occupied by objects that are no longer reachable from any GC root — roots include local variables currently on the stack, static fields, and CPU registers holding object references. A collection proceeds in three conceptual phases: Mark, where the GC starts from every root and recursively traces every reference reachable from them, marking each object it finds as still alive; Sweep, where every object on the heap that was not marked alive is reclaimed, since nothing reachable points to it anymore; and Compact, where the surviving objects are physically slid together in memory to eliminate the gaps left behind by sweeping, which both prevents heap fragmentation and lets future allocations remain a cheap, sequential 'bump the pointer' operation rather than a search for a suitably-sized free gap. To make this affordable, the GC organizes objects into generations based on how many collections they've survived: Generation 0 holds newly allocated objects and is collected very frequently and very cheaply, an assumption that pays off because empirically most objects die young (the 'generational hypothesis'); Generation 1 acts as a buffer holding Gen 0 survivors and is collected less often; Generation 2 holds long-lived objects — caches, singletons, static-held data — and is collected rarely, since a Gen 2 collection is a full, comparatively expensive collection across the entire live object graph; the separate Large Object Heap (LOH) holds objects at least 85,000 bytes, is collected together with Gen 2 collections, and — unlike the other generations — is not compacted by default, which historically made large allocations more prone to fragmentation, though this can be configured. An object surviving a given generation's collection is promoted to the next generation up, on the theory that objects which have already lived a while are statistically more likely to keep living. Two frequently tested follow-ups: first, the GC only manages memory — it has no concept of unmanaged resources like open file handles, database connections, or network sockets, and cleaning those up reliably requires implementing IDisposable and consuming the type via using, since the GC's timing is non-deterministic and cannot be relied upon for prompt release of scarce external resources; second, you should essentially never call GC.Collect() manually in production code, because it forces an immediate, full, disruptive stop-the-world collection across all generations, which usually degrades performance rather than improving it by prematurely promoting objects and interrupting normal generational behavior — it exists almost exclusively for diagnostics, memory-leak investigation, and benchmarking scenarios where you deliberately want to force a clean baseline. This all ties directly back to why allocation-heavy patterns matter for performance: boxing, ArrayList usage, and string concatenation in loops all increase the volume of garbage the GC has to trace and sweep, and finalizers are avoided specifically because any object with one is forced onto a separate finalization queue, requiring an extra GC cycle before its memory can actually be reclaimed.

codeExample.explanation: Short-lived temp allocations are cheaply collected in Gen 0, while a long-lived cache object survives collections and gets promoted toward Gen 2, which is collected far less often but much more expensively.

mistakes: Calling GC.Collect() in production code, forcing a disruptive full collection that usually hurts rather than helps performance.
Assuming the GC cleans up unmanaged resources like file handles or DB connections -- it manages memory only; IDisposable + using is required for those.
Writing unnecessary finalizers, which force objects onto the finalization queue and delay their actual collection by a full extra GC cycle.
Believing Gen 2 collections are as cheap and frequent as Gen 0 -- Gen 2 collections are comparatively rare and expensive full collections.
Ignoring allocation-heavy patterns (boxing, ArrayList, loop string concatenation) as if they had no cost, when each one adds real GC pressure and collection frequency.

followUps.question: How does GC relate to performance problems?
followUps.answer: Collections pause the application. More allocation -> more collections -> more pauses. That's why boxing, ArrayList, and string concatenation in loops matter, and why finalizers are avoided (they force a second GC cycle per object).

followUps.question: Why isn't the Large Object Heap compacted by default?
followUps.answer: Moving very large objects during compaction is itself expensive, so historically the LOH is swept but not compacted by default, which can lead to fragmentation over time with many large allocations of varying sizes; GCSettings.LargeObjectHeapCompactionMode can request a one-time compaction when genuinely needed.
